sections.h2: Which Tennessee counties follow the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act?
sections.html:
Only the larger counties follow it. The act in Tennessee Code Title 66, Chapter 28 applies in counties with a population above 75,000 under the 2010 federal census. A Tennessee Courts presentation on residential evictions lists these counties: Anderson, Blount, Bradley, Davidson, Greene, Hamilton, Knox, Madison, Maury, Montgomery, Putnam, Rutherford, Sevier, Shelby, Sullivan, Sumner, Washington, Williamson and Wilson.

Every other county falls under Tennessee Code section 66-7-101 and following. The presentation says only four sections of that older law actually apply: section 109 on termination of tenancy, 110 on tenants with disabilities, 111 on service and support animals, and 112 on domestic abuse.

How the two Tennessee landlord tenant regimes differ. Source: Tennessee Courts residential evictions presentation.

Late fee cap10 percent of the rent past dueNot addressed by the four applicable sections

Check which column your rental belongs in before you send any notice or promise any date. The county clerk or a local attorney can confirm it, and the answer changes what a notice must say.

sections.h2: What notices must a Tennessee landlord give?
sections.html:
In a URLTA county, a landlord facing a material breach can deliver a written notice that the lease ends in 14 days unless the tenant fixes the problem. If the same act or omission recurs within six months, a seven day written notice is enough. Section 66-28-505 covers these steps, and the Tennessee Courts presentation adds a three day notice for violence, threats and unsanitary conditions.

  • Month-to-month tenancy: either side ends it by written notice at least 30 days before the periodic rental date named in the notice.
  • Week-to-week tenancy: written notice at least 10 days before the termination date.
  • Repairs a tenant makes to cure a breach must be requested in writing and authorized in writing by the landlord before the work starts.
  • A holdover tenant who stays without consent after the lease ends can be sued for possession, back rent and reasonable attorney fees.

The presentation stresses that the owner must rely on the reasons stated in the notice when the case reaches court. If new misconduct happens after the notice goes out, the landlord must send an additional notice. For subsidized housing, written notice is required, and federal rules may differ from state law.

sections.h2: What happens to a tenant's lease when the landlord sells the house?
sections.html:
The statute speaks to the seller's liability and not to whether the tenant must leave. Under section 66-28-305, a landlord who sells to a good faith bona fide purchaser is relieved of liability under the rental agreement for events after the landlord gives the tenant written notice of the sale and transfers the security deposit to the buyer. Without that notice and transfer, the seller stays on the hook.

Section 66-28-302 requires a landlord to give the tenant the name and address of the property manager and of an owner or agent for service of notices, and it says that duty is enforceable against any successor landlord, owner or manager. A buyer who takes a rented house inherits that disclosure duty.

  • Tell the tenant in writing about the conveyance and about where the deposit went.
  • Hand the buyer the lease, the deposit and the tenant's contact details.
  • Do not count on an outright termination right because of the sale. Ask the county clerk, a local attorney or the court that handles detainer warrants what notice your lease and county require.

Showings have rules too. A tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent for the landlord to show the premises to actual or prospective purchasers, but the landlord may not abuse access or use it to harass. Section 66-28-403 lists the only situations in which a landlord may enter without the tenant's consent, such as an emergency or a court order.

sections.h2: How are Tennessee security deposits handled?
sections.html:
In URLTA counties, section 66-28-301 requires a landlord to hold every deposit in an account used only for that purpose, at a bank or lender regulated by Tennessee or the federal government. The landlord must tell the tenant where that account is when the lease is signed and the deposit is paid, though the account number need not be given.

  • The tenant may inspect the unit for damage that would justify a charge against the deposit, and the landlord can ask the tenant to be present.
  • A landlord who skipped the separate account or the damage listing cannot keep any part of the deposit.
  • Damage found after the inspection can be recovered only if the landlord discovered it within 30 days after the tenant left, or within seven days after a new tenant took possession, whichever comes first.
  • If the tenant owes nothing and a refund is due, the landlord mails a notice of the refund to the last known address. Unclaimed after 60 days, the landlord may take it out of the account.

A landlord who sells must pass the deposit to the buyer to gain the release described above. Record the amount in the closing paperwork so both sides agree on the figure.

sections.h2: How does a Tennessee eviction case move through court?
sections.html:
A landlord files a detainer warrant in general sessions court. The presentation lists three types: forcible entry and detainer under section 29-18-102, forcible detainer under 29-18-103 and unlawful detainer under 29-18-104.

  • Service: the summons can go to any adult found in possession, or to a party named in the lease. Personal service supports a money judgment.
  • Posting: after three attempts on three different dates, documented on the warrant, service can be made by posting a copy on the door and mailing one, at least six days before the hearing. Posting supports possession only, not a money judgment.
  • Continuances: the maximum is 15 days unless the parties agree, the landlord consents, or no court is being held.
  • Appeal: a defendant has ten days to appeal to circuit court and must post bond. A certiorari route to circuit court runs 30 days and needs a meritorious reason and bond.
  • Writ of possession: when the landlord wins, the writ is executed and the landlord restored to possession immediately.

If a defendant appeals without posting the required bond, the landlord does not have to post one to obtain possession. The landlord is also entitled to interest on the judgment from the judgment date if the defendant's appeal fails.

sections.h2: What protections apply to domestic abuse victims in a rental?
sections.html:
The URLTA and the older law use identical wording, in sections 66-28-205 and 66-28-517 for URLTA counties and 66-7-109 and 66-7-112 elsewhere. If domestic abuse is the reason a tenancy could be ended, only the perpetrator may be evicted. The landlord may not evict the victim, minor children or innocent occupants, and the perpetrator stays financially liable.

A landlord may remove the perpetrator from the lease and have the remaining adult tenants qualify for a new agreement. The victim and the other adult tenants must agree in writing not to let the perpetrator return. A tenant who is a domestic abuse, sexual assault or stalking victim can also request release from the lease by written notice, with a release date agreed within 30 days and a copy of either a valid order of protection after a hearing or documents showing a criminal charge.

A seller whose tenancy involves an order of protection should get legal advice before serving any notice.

faqs.q: Does the URLTA apply in my Tennessee county?
faqs.a: It applies in counties with more than 75,000 residents under the 2010 census. The Tennessee Courts presentation lists 19, including Davidson, Shelby, Knox, Hamilton and Rutherford. If your county is not listed, the shorter Title 66, Chapter 7 law applies, so confirm with your county clerk before sending notices.

faqs.q: How much notice does a landlord give to end a month-to-month lease?
faqs.a: At least 30 days before the periodic rental date named in the notice, in writing, under section 66-28-512 for URLTA counties. A week-to-week tenancy needs 10 days. Outside URLTA counties the courts presentation lists 14, 30 and three day notices, so check which one fits your situation.

faqs.q: Can a Tennessee landlord charge a late fee?
faqs.a: In URLTA counties, yes, up to 10 percent of the rent past due, and only after the five day grace period. The grace period does not count Sundays or legal holidays. The presentation lists no late fee cap for other counties, so check your lease.

faqs.q: Does selling the house cancel the tenant's lease?
faqs.a: The statute does not say a sale cancels a lease. Section 66-28-305 relieves a seller of later liability once the tenant receives written notice and the deposit goes to the buyer. Ask a local attorney or the clerk what notice your county requires for ending the lease.

faqs.q: How long does a Tennessee eviction take?
faqs.a: The statutes set no single timeline. Posted service must happen at least six days before the hearing, continuances are limited to 15 days, and a tenant has ten days to appeal. If the tenant appeals without bond, the landlord can still obtain possession.
